hook: Andrew Feldman has built two companies around the same conviction, that general-purpose processors are the wrong tool for specialized workloads. He first proved it with SeaMicro, a microserver startup he founded in 2007 that AMD acquired in 2012 for roughly 334 million dollars. He then co-founded Cerebras Systems in 2015 to apply the same logic to AI, building the Wafer-Scale Engine, a single chip roughly the size of a dinner plate designed specifically to keep AI training data close to compute instead of shuttling it between separate processors. As Cerebras CEO, Feldman has positioned wafer-scale computing as an alternative to clusters of GPUs for large-scale AI training and inference.

standing.record: The records add up to a career built on specialized computing rather than general-purpose processors. Feldman founded SeaMicro in 2007, a maker of energy-efficient microserver technology for cloud data centers, and AMD acquired it in February 2012 for approximately 334 million dollars. After the acquisition he served as General Manager of AMD's Data Center Server Solutions business. He then co-founded Cerebras Systems in 2015 to apply the same logic to AI, and the company built the Wafer-Scale Engine, a single chip roughly the size of a dinner plate designed to keep AI training data close to compute instead of shuttling it between separate processors. The site's company records list Cerebras in San Francisco with a founding year of 2016, and they leave funding and valuation blank. The records contain no lawsuits and no news stories naming Feldman or his companies.
standing.standing: Andrew Feldman stands as co-founder and CEO of Cerebras Systems, according to the records. The site lists him as an executive of Cerebras and as a founder of Cerebras. The profile says he co-founded the company in 2015 with Gary Lauterbach, Michael James, Sean Lie, and Jean-Philippe Fricker, while the company records list Cerebras as founded in 2016. The records show he has positioned wafer-scale computing as an alternative to clusters of GPUs for large-scale AI training and inference. They also show Cerebras built the Wafer-Scale Engine, a single chip built for AI training and inference rather than general-purpose computing. The records do not provide funding or valuation figures for Cerebras.
